name: Learn: Gateway API
objective: CKA › Services & Networking (20%, 2025). Goal: route HTTP with the Gateway API — GatewayClass, Gateway, and HTTPRoute — the successor to Ingress.
description: Learn the Gateway API step by step — the modern, role-oriented replacement for Ingress. Install the CRDs, define a GatewayClass, stand up a Gateway with an HTTP listener, attach an HTTPRoute to a backend Service, then contrast the same routing expressed as an Ingress.

questions.title: Install the Gateway API CRDs
questions.teach:
The Gateway API isn't built into Kubernetes — it ships as a set of **CRDs you install**. Until they're applied, the cluster doesn't know what a `Gateway` or `HTTPRoute` is. Installing CRDs from a release manifest is itself a common cluster task.

**The core resources (all in group `gateway.networking.k8s.io`):**
- `GatewayClass` (cluster-scoped) — the infrastructure template.
- `Gateway` — the listener/entry point.
- `HTTPRoute` (plus `TCPRoute`, `TLSRoute`, `GRPCRoute`, `UDPRoute`) — the routing rules.
- `ReferenceGrant` — permits cross-namespace references (e.g. a route in one ns pointing at a Service in another).

**Release channels:** the project ships two bundles — `standard` (stable: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, ReferenceGrant) and `experimental` (adds TCP/TLS/UDP routes and alpha fields). Install the one that matches what you need.

**Exam gotchas:**
- A CRD's `metadata.name` MUST be `<plural>.<group>` — here `gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io`. The CR's own `apiVersion` is `<group>/<version>` (e.g. `gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`).
- `apply` the manifest, then confirm the CRD reaches the **Established** condition (`kubectl get crd ... -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'`) before creating CRs — applying CRD + CR in one shot can race.
- CRDs are cluster-scoped; the objects they define may be Namespaced (Gateway, HTTPRoute) or Cluster (GatewayClass).
- Installing CRDs alone gives you the *API types*, not a working data plane — you still need a controller (next steps).
questions.prompt:
Install the Gateway API CRDs. The standard-channel manifest has been staged at `/tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml`. Apply it so the `GatewayClass`/`Gateway`/`HTTPRoute` types exist.

Target: the `gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io` CRD is installed and Established.
questions.hint: `kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml`, then `kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f /tmp/gateway-api-crds.yaml
kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io

questions.title: GatewayClass — the infrastructure template
questions.teach:
A **GatewayClass** is cluster-scoped and names the **controller** that will implement any `Gateway` referencing it — via its `spec.controllerName` field. It is analogous to an `IngressClass` (which names a controller via `spec.controller`).

The `controllerName` is just an identifier the controller watches for (e.g. `example.com/gateway-controller`); in this learn lab there is no running controller, so your Gateways will not get a real address — but the API objects are created and validated exactly as on a real cluster.

**How Gateways pick a class — three analogues to Ingress:**
- A `Gateway` selects its class by exact name in `spec.gatewayClassName` (there is no "default GatewayClass" mechanism like IngressClass's `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class` annotation — the reference is always explicit).
- `controllerName` is immutable once set and must be a domain-prefixed path.
- Optional `spec.parametersRef` points at an implementation-specific config object (CRD or ConfigMap) for controller tuning.

**Exam gotchas:**
- GatewayClass is **cluster-scoped** — no namespace. Many `Gateway`s across namespaces can share one GatewayClass.
- `kubectl create` has **no generator** for Gateway API objects — you must write YAML (or `kubectl create -f`/`apply -f`). `kubectl explain gatewayclass --recursive` is your friend when you forget a field.
- Watch the `Accepted` status condition — a real controller sets it; a wrong/unknown `controllerName` leaves the class unaccepted and its Gateways stuck.
- Deleting a GatewayClass that Gateways still reference leaves those Gateways orphaned (no controller).
questions.prompt:
Create a `GatewayClass` named `kindlab-gc` with any `controllerName` (for example `kindlab.io/gateway-controller`).

Target: `kubectl get gatewayclass kindlab-gc` succeeds and the object has a non-empty `spec.controllerName`.
questions.hint: Apply a manifest: `kind: GatewayClass`, `apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`, `metadata.name: kindlab-gc`, `spec.controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: kindlab-gc
spec:
  controllerName: kindlab.io/gateway-controller
EOF
kubectl get gatewayclass kindlab-gc

questions.title: Gateway — a listener for traffic
questions.teach:
A **Gateway** is the running entry point. It references a `GatewayClass` via `spec.gatewayClassName` and declares one or more **listeners** — each a `name`, `protocol` (HTTP/HTTPS/TCP/TLS/UDP), and `port`. This is where `Ingress` and the Gateway API diverge most: listeners are first-class, typed objects instead of annotations.

**Listener variations:**
- `protocol: HTTP` on `port: 80` (plaintext), or `protocol: HTTPS`/`TLS` which requires a `tls` block — `tls.mode: Terminate` (default) with `certificateRefs` to a TLS Secret, or `tls.mode: Passthrough` (no cert; hand the raw TLS to the backend).
- A single Gateway can hold **multiple listeners** (e.g. :80 HTTP and :443 HTTPS), each distinguished by its unique `name` and optional `hostname`.
- `allowedRoutes` controls which namespaces may attach routes: `from: Same` (default — Gateway's own ns), `All`, or `Selector` (match namespaces by label). You can also restrict `allowedRoutes.kinds`.

**Exam gotchas:**
- Listener `name`s must be **unique** within a Gateway; `port`+`protocol`+`hostname` combos must not collide.
- TLS termination needs a real Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls`; a missing/ wrong-type cert leaves the listener not `Programmed`.
- Cross-namespace routes require `allowedRoutes` to permit the route's namespace **and** a `ReferenceGrant` if the route points at a Service in another namespace.
- The Gateway gets an `.status.addresses` IP/hostname only once a controller programs it — no controller, no address (as in this lab).
- `Gateway` is **namespaced**; create it in the intended namespace (`gw-learn` here).
questions.prompt:
In namespace `gw-learn`, create a `Gateway` named `web-gw` that references class `kindlab-gc` and has an HTTP listener on port `80`.

Target: Gateway `web-gw` exists in `gw-learn`, references `kindlab-gc`, and has a listener with `protocol: HTTP` on `port: 80`.
questions.hint: `spec.gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc`, then `spec.listeners: [{ name: http, protocol: HTTP, port: 80 }]`. Apply with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gw
  namespace: gw-learn
spec:
  gatewayClassName: kindlab-gc
  listeners:
  - name: http
    protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
EOF
kubectl get gateway web-gw -n gw-learn

verification.description: Gateway 'web-gw' references kindlab-gc with an HTTP listener on 80

questions.title: HTTPRoute — attach routing rules
questions.teach:
An **HTTPRoute** binds to a Gateway through `spec.parentRefs` and describes how to match and forward requests via `spec.rules`. Each rule has `matches` and `backendRefs` (the target Services + ports). You can also set top-level `spec.hostnames`.

**Match types (a rule's `matches` can combine several):**
- `path` with `type: PathPrefix` (default), `Exact`, or `RegularExpression`.
- `headers` (Exact/RegularExpression), `queryParams`, and `method` (GET/POST…). Within one match element the conditions are **AND**ed; multiple match elements in a rule are **OR**ed.

**Backend & traffic variations:**
- Multiple `backendRefs` with `weight:` fields do **traffic splitting / canary** natively — no vendor annotations needed (the big win over Ingress).
- `filters` rewrite/redirect/modify requests: `RequestHeaderModifier`, `RequestRedirect`, `URLRewrite`, `RequestMirror`, `ResponseHeaderModifier`.
- Backends can be `TCPRoute`/`GRPCRoute`/`TLSRoute` instead of HTTP for non-HTTP traffic.

**Exam gotchas:**
- `parentRefs` can target a specific **listener** via `sectionName` and may include a `namespace` for cross-ns attachment.
- Pointing at a Service in **another namespace** needs a `ReferenceGrant` in the Service's namespace — without it the backend ref is not permitted (the route's `ResolvedRefs` condition goes `False`, reason `RefNotPermitted`).
- Check `.status.parents[].conditions` for `Accepted` and `ResolvedRefs`; a typo'd Service name shows up as `ResolvedRefs: False`.
- This is the app-developer's piece: the operator owns the Gateway, you own the route. A Service `hello` (ClusterIP on port 80) has been seeded in `gw-learn` for you to point at.
questions.prompt:
In `gw-learn`, create an `HTTPRoute` named `web-route` that attaches to Gateway `web-gw` (parentRef), matches hostname `hello.example.com` with path prefix `/`, and forwards to the `hello` Service on port `80`.

Target: HTTPRoute `web-route` has a `parentRef` to `web-gw` and a `backendRef` to Service `hello`.
questions.hint: `spec.parentRefs: [{ name: web-gw }]`, `spec.hostnames: [hello.example.com]`, and a rule with `matches[0].path.type: PathPrefix`, `value: /`, plus `backendRefs: [{ name: hello, port: 80 }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: web-route
  namespace: gw-learn
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: web-gw
  hostnames:
  - hello.example.com
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /
    backendRefs:
    - name: hello
      port: 80
EOF
kubectl get httproute web-route -n gw-learn -o yaml

verification.description: HTTPRoute 'web-route' references web-gw (parentRef) and backend Service hello

questions.title: Contrast with Ingress
questions.teach:
The Gateway API replaces **Ingress**, so it helps to express the same routing both ways. An Ingress uses a single resource with `spec.rules[].http.paths[]`, each mapping a path to a `backend.service`. Compared to the Gateway API it is simpler but less expressive — no typed listeners, no clean role separation, and traffic-splitting/header-matching need vendor annotations.

**Ingress essentials (and how they map to Gateway API):**
- `spec.ingressClassName` → picks the controller (≈ `gatewayClassName`). One class may be marked default via the `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"` annotation.
- `pathType` must be set per path: `Prefix`, `Exact`, or `ImplementationSpecific` (≈ HTTPRoute `path.type`).
- `spec.tls[]` references a TLS Secret per host (≈ listener `tls.certificateRefs`).
- `spec.defaultBackend` catches unmatched requests (no direct HTTPRoute equivalent — you'd use a catch-all rule).
- `kubectl create ingress NAME --rule="host/path*=svc:port"` is the fast generator; the `*` makes it a `Prefix` path.

**Exam gotchas:**
- An Ingress (like a Gateway) does nothing without a running **ingress controller** — the object can exist yet serve no traffic.
- `--rule` path **with** a trailing `*` → `pathType: Prefix`; **without** → `Exact`. Easy to get wrong under time pressure.
- Host-based vs path-based rules, and annotations (`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/...`) are controller-specific — not portable, unlike Gateway API filters.
- Build an Ingress for the **same** `hello` Service so both objects coexist — the HTTPRoute from step 4 and a classic Ingress, side by side.
questions.prompt:
In `gw-learn`, create an `Ingress` named `web-ing` that routes host `hello.example.com` path `/` to Service `hello` port `80`.

Target: both the HTTPRoute `web-route` (from step 4) and the Ingress `web-ing` exist in `gw-learn`, each pointing at the `hello` Service.
questions.hint: `kubectl create ingress web-ing -n gw-learn --rule="hello.example.com/*=hello:80"` is the quickest way, or write the YAML with `spec.rules[].http.paths[].backend.service.name: hello`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create ingress web-ing -n gw-learn --rule="hello.example.com/*=hello:80"
kubectl get ingress web-ing -n gw-learn
kubectl get httproute web-route -n gw-learn   # both exist: same routing, two APIs

verification.description: both HTTPRoute web-route and Ingress web-ing route to the hello Service
